newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Coffee monitors weather, cocoa firm.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Coffee monitors weather, cocoa firm.

text.p: Coffee traders shift their attention this week to Brazilian weather news after digesting last week's surprise decision by key producers to extend their current cartel-style export quotas for 12 more months.
Elsewhere on the soft commodity front, LIFFE cocoa may drift higher and at the upper hand of a wider trading band between 980 and 1,060 stg basis July.
In white sugar futures, the front-month August is expected to retain most of its recent strength ahead of summer, the end-tail of European availability.

Both London and New York futures coffee reversed their downward correction after the Association of Coffee Producing Countries agreed to limit exports to 52.75 million 60-kg bags for one year from July 1.
Roasters and consumers had earlier expected the ACPC, led by Brazil, to loosen their current curbs in view of the tight supply situation and the steep increase in prices since January.
The ACPC news sent New York and London to new highs this week. New York's July futures was driven to new life-of-contract highs of $2.65 per lb on Thursday, driven by speculative buying.
London's robusta futures raced up to $2,145 per tonne on Thursday.
The ACPC decision has been described as outrageous by some major roasters, saying that the historically high bean prices were bound to significantly cut world consumption.
ACPC officials defended the move, saying that their goal was to ensure prices remained at a level renumerative to producers and at the same time ensured sufficient supply to the market.
The coffee market will now track weather news from Brazil as the country enters the critical frost season in June and July.
"Weather is still a worry," said one trader. Any threat of frost in the coffee belt would send prices higher.
Some traders speculated that prices could eventually test $5 per lb in New York if there is a widespread damage to the coffee trees.
Without any crop-damaging frosts, the market will turn lower again although the nearby months could hold well above $2.
London's robustas are seen over-valued but July could find support at just above $2,000 in the short term, traders said.
London faces further origin selling while roasters are said to be pretty covered.

In cocoa, the July contract has been mostly in a range between 1,000 and 1,035 stg per tonne, but some traders and analysts were looking for July to slowly inch up toward the upper end of a wider trading band between the April 9 low of 980 and about 1,060.
They said July position might drift higher in the next couple of weeks.
Though most traders said it was still too early to speculate on the new crop, they said talk that early settings in the Ivory Coast were low would likely keep prices underpinned in the near-term.
Cocoa also looked resililent technically. After testing and failing at 1,060 twice before, analysts said a third attempt could be promising within the next couple of weeks.
They said the third try could ultimately be the one that succeeds in breaking 1,060 to get July up into a new trading range.

But some analysts were concerned about the recent low turnover plaguing the market. They said July would have a difficult time gathering momentum and strength to break 1,060, a level not seen since late April.
Traders also said continued origin sales would likely dampen enthusiasm to the upside.
Ghana was said to be selling against current and new crop while Ivory Coast, considered already well-sold for the current crop, is concentrating its sales against the new crop.
Initial support rests at 1,000, with strong and crucial support pegged at 980.

In white sugar, the spot August contract is expected to retain most of its recent strength as trade players seem eager to avoid being short of the key summer delivery month -- the tail-end of European availability.
"I think being long of August/October is what most trade people would like to be," said one market source.
But producer pricing is believed to be keeping a lid on the market and traders said they thought the limit of the upside potential was around $324.00.
Persistent talk of Russian purchases and the fortunes of the large Brazilian raws delivery into the Black Sea region are expected to remain the main physical talking points this week.
Traders said the alleged Russian buying interest was still supporting nearby futures even though the purchases have yet to be confirmed.
"The buyers aren't in too much of a hurry to pay up and they're sitting there trying to pick away at it but the Russian interest is keeping the market on the dboil," said one.
"While that's in the background, the market isn't necessarily going to come down but...I don't think it's going to run away on the upside."
While trade players dominated much of the whites market last week, the return of the London fraternity from New York's sugar week should bolster activity. -- London newsroom +44 171 5424985
